slides.text: Calculus measures angles in **radians**. A full turn is $2pi$, so half a turn is $pi$, which is 180°. How many degrees is $frac{pi}{2}$?
slides.explain: $frac{pi}{2}$ is a quarter turn, 90°. To convert, remember one fact: $pi$ = 180°.

slides.text: Here is the unit circle: radius 1, centered at the origin. At every angle, **cosine is the x-coordinate and sine is the y-coordinate** of the point. Tap these three angles and watch both.
slides.after: Only three numbers ever show up: $frac{1}{2}$, $frac{sqrt2}{2}$ and $frac{sqrt3}{2}$, smallest to largest. Sine climbs through them while cosine comes down.

slides.hint: $frac{pi}{6}$ is 30°: a low point, so its height is the small number.
slides.explain: At $frac{pi}{6}$ the point is far to the right and not very high: $(frac{sqrt3}{2}, frac{1}{2})$.

slides.text: The other three quadrants reuse the same values. Only the **signs** change. Tap these and watch the signs.
slides.after: Left of the $y$-axis, cosine is negative. Below the $x$-axis, sine is negative. That is all there is to it.

slides.text: Now with no labels. Tap the point at $theta = frac{2pi}{3}$.
slides.hint: $frac{pi}{3}$ is 60°, so $frac{2pi}{3}$ is 120°: a little past straight up.
slides.explain: Angles start on the positive $x$-axis and go counterclockwise. 120° lands in the second quadrant.

slides.hint: $pi$ is half a turn. Where is the point?
slides.explain: Half a turn puts the point at $(-1, 0)$, and cosine is the $x$-coordinate.
